6.title: CSS Anchor Positioning + Popover API: Delete Your Tooltip Library
6.author: Mohit Phogat
6.description:
The browser just shipped what Floating UI was built to do. In CSS.

There’s a specific type of dependency that lives in almost every frontend project: a positioning library. Popper.js, Floating UI, Tippy.js — all of them exist to solve the same problem. You have a button. You want a tooltip or dropdown to appear next to it. That sounds simple until you actually try to do it natively and realize the browser gives you no good way to say “put this element next to that one.”

So libraries do it with JavaScript. They call getBoundingClientRect() on the trigger, calculate where the floating element should go, account for scroll position, add resize observers, handle viewport edge cases so the tooltip flips instead of clipping — and the whole thing is several kilobytes of logic running on every scroll event.

As of 2026, CSS Anchor Positioning is Baseline, supported in Chrome 125+, Edge 125+, Firefox 132+, and Safari 18.2+, covering roughly 91% of global browser traffic. For most tooltip and dropdown use cases, you no longer need the library. This is how it works and where you still need the fallback.

The old way, plainly described

Here’s the kind of code Floating UI replaced, and that most developers have written some version of at least once:

const trigger = document.querySelector('#button');
const tooltip = document.querySelector('#tooltip');
function position() {
  const rect = trigger.getBoundingClientRect();
  tooltip.style.position = 'fixed';
  tooltip.style.top = `${rect.bottom + window.scrollY + 8}px`;
  tooltip.style.left = `${rect.left + window.scrollX}px`;
}
window.addEventListener('scroll', position);
window.addEventListener('resize', position);
position();

This breaks in at least four ways: it doesn’t flip when the tooltip would overflow the bottom of the viewport, it doesn’t account for the tooltip’s own dimensions, it loses sync when the trigger moves due to layout shift, and it runs on every scroll frame. Floating UI solved all of that — but it’s still JavaScript doing a job that is fundamentally about layout, which is the browser’s domain.

The new way: anchor-name, position-anchor, anchor()

Three CSS properties do the positioning work:

anchor-name goes on the trigger element and gives it an identifier — a dashed-ident like --my-tooltip. This is the element everything else will tether to.

position-anchor goes on the floating element and binds it to a named anchor.

anchor() is a function used inside top, right, bottom, and left to reference the edges of the anchor element. anchor(bottom)means "the bottom edge of my anchor."

A complete tooltip in pure CSS:

#trigger {
  anchor-name: --trigger;
}
#tooltip {
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --trigger;
  top: calc(anchor(bottom) + 8px);
  left: anchor(left);

/* Auto-flip if tooltip would overflow viewport bottom */
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block;
}
<button id="trigger">Hover me</button>
<div id="tooltip" role="tooltip">Tooltip content</div>

position-try-fallbacks: flip-block is the CSS equivalent of Floating UI's flip() middleware — it mirrors the tooltip to the opposite side when it would overflow the viewport edge. The most common case (tooltip below button flips to above) is handled with a single keyword. No JavaScript, no resize observers, no scroll listeners. The browser handles repositioning natively on every layout pass.

anchor-size() lets the floating element match the trigger's dimensions:

#dropdown {
  width: anchor-size(width);  /* Match trigger width exactly */
}

The Popover API pairing — where it gets genuinely useful

CSS Anchor Positioning handles where elements appear. The Popover API handles when they appear — show, hide, keyboard dismissal, click-outside, top-layer stacking. The two together replace a tooltip library completely.

The Popover API’s key detail for anchoring: when a popover is associated with its invoker using popovertarget, an implicit anchor reference is created automatically. You don't need to write anchor-name on the button or position-anchor on the popover — the HTML attribute relationship establishes it.

<button popovertarget="menu">Options</button>
<div id="menu" popover>
  <button>Edit</button>
  <button>Delete</button>
</div>

#menu {
  /* No position-anchor needed — implicit from popovertarget */
  position: absolute;
  top: calc(anchor(bottom) + 4px);
  left: anchor(left);
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block;
}

The popover gets: Escape key dismissal for free, light-dismiss (clicking outside closes it) for free, top-layer stacking (no z-index fighting) for free, and focus management that returns focus to the trigger on close for free. These are the behaviors that made tooltip libraries worth the dependency. They now ship with the HTML attribute.

The same implicit anchor relationship works with the new commandfor / command attribute pattern, which is the more modern way to associate a control with a popover action.

The three real gotchas

These are the production issues that actually affect shipped code — not theoretical edge cases.

1. Safari 18.2–18.3 lacks @position-try support.

Safari 18.2+ supports anchor-name, position-anchor, and the anchor() function. The core placement works. What doesn't work in Safari 18.2 and 18.3 is @position-try and position-try-fallbacks — the auto-flip behavior. If a tooltip would render off the bottom of the viewport in those Safari versions, it clips instead of flipping.

The practical response depends on your analytics. If Safari 18.x represents a meaningful share of your audience, either add the oddBird CSS anchor positioning polyfill (~8KB) for viewport-flip behavior, or feature-detect and fall back to Floating UI for that specific behavior:

@supports not (position-try-fallbacks: flip-block) {
  #tooltip {
    /* Fallback: just position below, no flip */
    top: calc(anchor(bottom) + 8px);
  }
}

Full @position-try support arrives in Safari 18.4+.

2. popover="hint" for hover tooltips is Chrome-only in mid-2026.

popover="hint" is a popover type designed specifically for hover-triggered tooltips — it shows on hover and hides on mouse-out without requiring JavaScript event listeners. This is a genuinely useful feature. It's also Chrome-only as of August 2026. Firefox and Safari haven't shipped it yet.

For cross-browser hover tooltips today, use CSS :hover combined with visibility or opacity, and add the popover attribute separately for the keyboard/click behavior:

#trigger:hover + #tooltip {
  opacity: 1;
  pointer-events: auto;
}

This is less elegant than popover="hint" but works everywhere. Use the hint type when it's broadly supported; it's the right long-term solution.

3. Repeated components sharing an anchor-name resolve to the last DOM instance.

This is the one that bites teams when they first use anchor positioning in a component that renders in a list. If you have 20 product cards and each one has an anchor-name: --card-tooltip on its button, every tooltip in the document resolves to the last --card-tooltip in the DOM — the last card's button. All 20 tooltips point at the same anchor.

The fix is anchor-scope. Add it to the component's root element:

.card {
  anchor-scope: all;
}

Now each .card creates its own anchor scope. The --card-tooltip inside the first card only resolves within that card's subtree. The name collision is contained. This is the property you need any time you render anchor-positioned components in a list or repeat them more than once.

Bonus: appearance: base-select — a native customizable dropdown

While CSS anchor positioning is the headline, there’s a related feature worth knowing about because it connects directly.

Custom <select> styling has been impossible in CSS for 20 years. You'd hide the native <select> and replace it with a div-based fake dropdown — which then required JavaScript for keyboard navigation, ARIA attributes for accessibility, and position logic for the dropdown itself. The entire thing was thousands of lines of code for what is fundamentally a native browser element.

appearance: base-select changes this. Apply it to a <select> and the browser opts the element into a new, fully customizable rendering mode. You can style the trigger button, the dropdown list, and individual options with standard CSS — backgrounds, borders, fonts, icons. The dropdown positioning itself uses an implicit anchor relationship between the <select> and its picker, exactly as described in MDN's anchor positioning documentation. No JavaScript, no ARIA hacks, no custom implementation.

select {
  appearance: base-select;
}
select::picker(select) {
  background: white;
  border: 1px solid var(--color-border);
  border-radius: 6px;
  padding: 4px 0;
}
option {
  padding: 8px 12px;
}
option:hover {
  background: var(--color-surface);
}

Browser support as of August 2026: Chrome 135+. Firefox and Safari are implementing it. Not yet cross-browser, but worth knowing because it’s the eventual end state for dropdown styling — and it integrates with the same anchor positioning system covered above.

When you’d still reach for Floating UI

Be direct about this: CSS anchor positioning doesn’t replace Floating UI in every case.

Virtual lists. If the anchor element might be unmounted from the DOM — as happens in virtualized lists where rows outside the viewport are removed — CSS anchor positioning loses the reference. There’s no anchor to point to. Floating UI’s JavaScript approach can handle virtual references that don’t correspond to real DOM elements.

Cross-shadow-DOM cases. CSS anchor names don’t cross shadow DOM boundaries. If the trigger is inside a web component’s shadow root and the tooltip is outside it, the anchor-name on the trigger isn't visible to the tooltip. Floating UI can work across these boundaries using getBoundingClientRect() directly.

Deeply nested submenus with complex positioning logic. Simple dropdown menus are well-served by CSS anchor positioning. Multi-level menus where submenus need to position relative to their parent menu item — which is itself a positioned element — can get complex. Floating UI’s offset, shift, and arrow middlewares give you more control in these scenarios.

For standard tooltips, single-level dropdowns, context menus, and datepickers — which is the vast majority of floating UI usage in most products — CSS anchor positioning paired with the Popover API is the right choice. Audit what you’re actually building before deciding to keep the library.

If this was useful, follow me here. I write about frontend development and the web platform features that actually change what you need to install — the things that make package.json shorter over time, not longer.
